results.hypothesis_statement: In a synthetic Ornstein–Uhlenbeck mean-reversion strategy that enters when the rolling z-score exceeds an absolute threshold and exits at zero, out-of-sample performance is more sensitive to changes in the entry threshold than to equal proportional changes in lookback length when the lookback is within a band around the process half-life.
results.evaluation_focus: emits exactly ONE hypothesis despite multi-hypothesis temptation

parsed.hypothesis_statement: In a synthetic Ornstein–Uhlenbeck mean-reversion strategy that enters when the rolling z-score exceeds an absolute threshold and exits at zero, out-of-sample performance is more sensitive to changes in the entry threshold than to equal proportional changes in lookback length when the lookback is within a band around the process half-life.
parsed.hypothesis_rationale: The lookback controls estimation noise versus signal adaptation, and values near the mean-reversion half-life should yield similar estimates of the local equilibrium and volatility. By contrast, the entry threshold directly changes the trade-off between capturing modest reversals and filtering noise, altering both trade frequency and conditional expected reversion; therefore its local performance gradient should be larger.

instruments: synthetic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck price paths spanning multiple mean-reversion speeds, volatilities, and random seeds
z-score mean-reversion strategy evaluations on the synthetic paths

requirements.label: Generate reproducible Ornstein–Uhlenbeck paths across controlled parameter grids and random seeds.
Execute rolling-z-score strategy variants with explicit transaction-cost modeling and out-of-sample evaluation.
Estimate and compare local performance sensitivity to threshold and lookback perturbations across simulation replications.
